extracted.intended_audience: independent inventors and people drafting their own patent applications
extracted.subtask_short: describing an invention in a patent application
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for inventors on how to write the specification and disclosure of a patent application so it fully, clearly, and exactly describes the invention and supports enforceable claims. Focuses on avoidable mistakes when inventors draft their own applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full, clear, and exact description
rubrics_metrics.description: The goal in a patent application is to provide a full, clear, and exact description of the invention in a way that particularly points out and distinctly identifies what the inventor believes he or she has invented and wants the patent to cover.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe the invention comprehensively so a reader can understand what is claimed and what the inventor regards as the invention. This is the statutory requirement for a patent specification; the disclosure must 'particularly point out and distinctly identify' the invention. Omit nothing material to understanding the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assume the reader knows (Assuming the Reader Knows is Dangerous)
rubrics_metrics.description: You absolutely positively cannot assume any particular familiarity with your invention; it is very dangerous to assume the reader will fill in ambiguous holes in the manner you desire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write for an intelligent audience with no particular expertise in your subject. Be specific and explicit; provide examples and concrete embodiments to flesh out descriptions. Anti-pattern: leaving key details implicit or relying on the reader to infer steps, structures, or relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow broad/generic language with specifics (generic + specifics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many inventors want to be as generic as possible to capture territory, but if you do that you need to realize the likelihood of obtaining a patent is very low unless you follow up with specifics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you use broad or functional language to capture scope, also include concrete examples, specific embodiments, and implementation details so the reader can truly comprehend the complexity and nuance of the invention. Scoring note: purely generic disclosure without enabling specifics is vulnerable to rejection or invalidation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assume an intelligent non-expert audience; choose words carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Always assume you are writing for and describing your invention to an intelligent audience, but an audience with no particular expertise. This should make you choose your words carefully to convey the most precise meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer clear, unambiguous terminology; define terms where necessary. Avoid jargon that requires domain knowledge to interpret. Be your own lexicographer when appropriate (see linked resources).

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe the invention as if to a blind person (verbal, step-by-step disclosure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Strive to describe your invention in words that inform — like a step-by-step how-to manual — so that someone who cannot see could still understand it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use detailed, sequential verbal descriptions of how components are arranged and how the invention operates. Drawings help but do not substitute for a thorough written disclosure. Exercise: try describing the invention to someone who is blind to reveal missing verbal detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use drawings but ensure the written disclosure is informative
rubrics_metrics.description: You will include drawings in your application, hopefully many drawings, that will facilitate understanding, but you really need to strive to describe your invention in words that inform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely solely on drawings; include accompanying textual explanation that points to and explains the drawings, elements, and interactions. Drawings are complementary to, not a replacement for, the written specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose wording to avoid literal misinterpretation (say what you mean)
rubrics_metrics.description: You need to choose your words carefully to make sure your words are exactly what you mean — what you say will be interpreted literally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully proofread for literal errors or imprecise phrasing that could render a claim meaningless (e.g., 'heat the dough to 450 degrees' vs 'heat the oven to 450 degrees'). Antipattern: sloppy or colloquial phrasing that changes legal effect when read literally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe structure, not just design purpose (Design Purpose NOT Enough)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explaining the design purpose is helpful, but is not enough for a patent application. A patent application absolutely must describe the structure of the device; describing how or why it will be used is not a substitute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide detailed structural descriptions of parts, how they connect, and their relationships. Avoid relying solely on functional descriptions or intended use as the basis for the disclosure. The specification should enable construction/operation, not merely state a goal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide exhaustive, instruction-manual level detail (explain obvious things)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain your invention with so much detail that you will bore the knowledgeable reader to death — explain everything, no matter how obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for 'instruction manual' detail and include variations and alternatives. Better to over-explain than to omit what seems obvious to you. This supports enablement and reduces ambiguity during examination or litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include examples and embodiments to flesh out concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider providing an example or two to help flesh out what it is you are describing — while not required examples can be particularly helpful in a patent application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use worked examples, specific parameter values, exemplary materials, or implementation steps to illustrate embodiments. Examples help satisfy enablement and illustrate the breadth/scope of claimed concepts.
